first_impression.reaction: Sophie here. The second sentence got me: 'Most guides online are written for British or American couples and talk about a Certificate of No Impediment, which Italy will not accept from you.' I've literally read two of those guides this month. Saying it's the Australian version and dating it 'as at October 2026' makes it feel like someone actually checked. I'm a lawyer, so I read the whole legal section properly. James would skim the takeaways and the table.

journey.quote: Most guides online are written for British or American couples and talk about a Certificate of No Impediment, which Italy will not accept from you.
journey.reaction: Good, straight away it tells me something the other guides got wrong. That's why I kept reading.

journey.quote: The Atto Notorio cannot be issued more than six months before the wedding, and you need four unrelated adult witnesses at the appointment.
journey.reaction: Four unrelated adults turning up at the consulate on a weekday is a real job. Exactly the kind of thing I'd want someone else to manage. Useful to know now, 14 months out.

journey.section: What the Atto Notorio is and where to get it
journey.quote: In Sydney, both of you attend with four witnesses who are not related to either of you, though they can be related to each other.
journey.reaction: We're in Sydney, so this is about us. The bit about the witnesses being allowed to be related to each other is the sort of fine print only someone who's done it would mention.

journey.section: What the Nulla Osta is and who signs it
journey.quote: Not published: how far ahead Rome and Milan release appointments, and whether a non-Australian partner attends. Your Wedded Advisor confirms both in writing before you book flights.
journey.reaction: I like that they say what they don't know instead of making it up. 'In writing' matters to me. But it does mean the trickiest booking in the whole process has no lead time on the page.

journey.section: Why a Certificate of No Impediment will not work in Italy
journey.quote: "Nulla Ostas sworn outside of Italy and Certificates of No Impediment are not valid for use in Italy."
journey.reaction: A direct quote from the Embassy. That's the kind of evidence I'd send to Mum to stop her forwarding me the wrong article.

journey.quote: On Sydney's list, two Australians with two certificates and two translations each can need eight apostilles.
journey.reaction: Eight apostilles. This is exactly the spreadsheet I don't want to be running at night. Honest, and it makes me want someone to handle it, but it doesn't say who does the running around: us or them.

journey.section: Step by step once you arrive in Italy
journey.quote: allow a working week rather than arriving two days out.
journey.reaction: Really practical, and it changes how we'd plan leave. But with 30-odd guests flying in from overseas, are we really going to be queueing at a Prefettura in Rome that same week? I'd want to know if someone comes with us.

journey.quote: Buy a revenue stamp (marca da bollo) at a tobacconist (tabaccaio) first.
journey.reaction: This is the insider detail I trust. Nobody would make that up.

journey.quote: Bagno a Ripoli does not provide one; finding the interpreter is up to you.
journey.reaction: 'Up to you' is the phrase that worries me. Is it up to us, or does the Wedded Advisor arrange the interpreter? Every planner says they're end-to-end, and this is where I'd find out if that's true.

journey.section: Step by step once you arrive in Italy
journey.quote: Bagno a Ripoli and Montespertoli ask non-resident foreign couples to sign their sworn declaration at least three days before the wedding.
journey.reaction: Bagno a Ripoli keeps coming up. I get that it's an example, but we haven't picked a region. I'd like to see one Amalfi or Lake Como comune too, so it doesn't read like a Florence-only guide.

journey.section: Your timeline, working back from the wedding date
journey.quote: The squeeze is in the middle. Both documents expire six months after signing, so a date that moves late can mean signing again.
journey.reaction: The table is the most useful thing on the page, and this line is the honest trade-off. I'd screenshot the table and send it to James.

journey.section: Marry legally in Australia, celebrate in Italy
journey.quote: Weigh [whether to marry legally abroad or hold a symbolic ceremony] before you commit.
journey.reaction: Honestly, after reading all of the above, a quick signing in Sydney and a symbolic ceremony in Italy sounds a lot easier. I'd have liked one or two lines here on what most couples like us actually do and why, not just a link.

journey.section: Is an Italian marriage recognised in Australia?
journey.quote: In NSW and Victoria, an overseas marriage certificate cannot be used to take your spouse's surname, so you apply for a change of name instead.
journey.reaction: Didn't know that and it affects me directly. Good catch.

journey.quote: Most official steps carry a fee, and amounts move with exchange rates or annual indexation.
journey.reaction: Then five bullets that all say 'a fee applies' and not one figure or range. I understand rates change, but a rough 'all-in paperwork is usually around X to Y AUD' is what I wanted. This is where I'd glaze over.

journey.section: Plan the paperwork with one person
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD and stays with you from the first document to the last dance.
journey.reaction: Time zone and AUD quotes are the two things I actually care about, so that lands. 'First document to the last dance' is a bit cute, but it isn't tacky.

unanswered_questions: What exactly does the Wedded Advisor do with the paperwork? Do they book the Nulla Osta appointment, organise the interpreter, and come with us to the Prefettura and comune, or do they just tell us what to do?
Roughly what does all the legal paperwork cost in AUD, as a range, including translations, apostilles, interpreter and comune fees?
How many days in Italy before the wedding do couples like us realistically need, and is there anyone with us on those days?
Which do most Australian couples actually choose, legal in Italy or legal at home plus a symbolic ceremony, and what are the trade-offs for a wedding of 60 to 90 guests?
Is there a real wedding where you handled the Italian legal ceremony for an Australian couple, with the venue and date?
How do the rules differ in the regions we're considering, like Lake Como or the Amalfi Coast, rather than just Bagno a Ripoli?

turn_offs_found.quote: Atto Notorio:** a consular fee applies, set by each consulate's tariff.
turn_offs_found.why: Vague pricing with no ranges. Every line in the cost section says a fee applies and none gives a number or range, so I still have no idea of the total.

would_share_with: James (partner): the key takeaways and the timeline table
Mum and Dad, since they're contributing: the Certificate of No Impediment section, so they stop sending the UK guides

cta_reaction.quote: [Speak with a Wedded Advisor about your paperwork timeline](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge), starting with your date and your comune.
cta_reaction.why: It's low-pressure, which I like. But we don't have a date or a comune yet, so it reads like it's for couples further along than us. And I still don't know whether 'Wedded Advisor' means they do the paperwork or just advise. I'd read one or two more posts and look for a real wedding before I enquire.

top_3_changes: Spell out what the Wedded Advisor physically does in each step (books the Nulla Osta appointment, finds the interpreter, comes to the Prefettura and comune). Right now it reads as 'confirms in writing', and I need to know it means 'handles it'.
Give at least an indicative AUD range for the total paperwork cost, flagged as approximate, instead of five lines saying 'a fee applies'.
Add one real Australian couple who married legally in Italy, with the venue, comune and date, plus a sentence on how many days before the wedding they arrived. That's what would make me enquire.
